claim: The biofilm transcription network in C. albicans is composed of seven 'master' transcription regulators (Bcr1, Brg1, Efg1, Flo8, Ndt80, Rob1, and Tec1).
source: In C. albicans, a complex transcription network regulates this process; it consists of seven 'master' transcription regulators (Bcr1, Brg1, Efg1, Flo8, Ndt80, Rob1, and Tec1) that control each other's expression and, collectively, bind to the control regions of more than a thousand target genes — around one-sixth of the total number of genes present in the genome of this species (Figure 1; Nobile et al., 2012; Fox et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Nobile et al., 2012; Fox et al., 2015) and reference to Figure 1.

claim: The seven master regulators collectively bind to the control regions of more than a thousand target genes, representing around one-sixth of the total number of genes in the C. albicans genome.
source: In C. albicans, a complex transcription network regulates this process; it consists of seven 'master' transcription regulators (Bcr1, Brg1, Efg1, Flo8, Ndt80, Rob1, and Tec1) that control each other's expression and, collectively, bind to the control regions of more than a thousand target genes — around one-sixth of the total number of genes present in the genome of this species (Figure 1; Nobile et al., 2012; Fox et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Nobile et al., 2012; Fox et al., 2015) and reference to Figure 1.

claim: All seven master regulators appear to be positive regulators that are required for normal biofilm development in C. albicans.
source: All of the seven regulators appear to be positive regulators that are required for normal biofilm development.
evidence: The claim is based on prior characterization of the regulators, as indicated by the context and citations in the manuscript.

claim: Genes that are highly expressed during biofilm formation in C. albicans are enriched for genes that are relatively young, having orthologs only in species closely related to C. albicans.
source: For example, genes that are highly expressed during biofilm formation are enriched for genes that are relatively young, meaning that they only have a clear ortholog in species closely related to C. albicans (Nobile et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Nobile et al., 2012).

claim: C. parapsilosis diverged from a last common ancestor with C. albicans nominally 70 million years ago.
source: C. parapsilosis diverged from a last common ancestor with C. albicans nominally 70 million years ago (Mishra et al., 2007; Butler et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Mishra et al., 2007; Butler et al., 2009).

claim: Six of the seven master regulators of biofilm formation in C. albicans have clear orthologs in C. parapsilosis.
source: Although six of the seven master regulators of biofilm formation in C. albicans have clear orthologs in C. parapsilosis, only two of them are required for biofilm formation in the latter species (Holland et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Holland et al., 2014).

claim: Only two of the seven master regulators are required for biofilm formation in C. parapsilosis.
source: Although six of the seven master regulators of biofilm formation in C. albicans have clear orthologs in C. parapsilosis, only two of them are required for biofilm formation in the latter species (Holland et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Holland et al., 2014).

claim: C. dubliniensis and C. tropicalis are more closely related to C. albicans than C. parapsilosis is.
source: Candida dubliniensis and Candida tropicalis are more closely related to C. albicans (see Figure 2) and are also known to form biofilms (Ramage et al., 2001; Silva et al., 2011; Pujol et al., 2015; Araújo et al., 2017; Dominguez et al., 2018; Kumari et al., 2018), but the regulatory circuits that control this process are largely unknown.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2 and citations to prior work (Ramage et al., 2001; Silva et al., 2011; Pujol et al., 2015; Araújo et al., 2017; Dominguez et al., 2018; Kumari et al., 2018).

claim: C. dubliniensis and C. tropicalis are known to form biofilms.
source: Candida dubliniensis and Candida tropicalis are more closely related to C. albicans (see Figure 2) and are also known to form biofilms (Ramage et al., 2001; Silva et al., 2011; Pujol et al., 2015; Araújo et al., 2017; Dominguez et al., 2018; Kumari et al., 2018), but the regulatory circuits that control this process are largely unknown.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Ramage et al., 2001; Silva et al., 2011; Pujol et al., 2015; Araújo et al., 2017; Dominguez et al., 2018; Kumari et al., 2018).

claim: The regulatory circuits that control biofilm formation in C. dubliniensis and C. tropicalis are largely unknown.
source: Candida dubliniensis and Candida tropicalis are more closely related to C. albicans (see Figure 2) and are also known to form biofilms (Ramage et al., 2001; Silva et al., 2011; Pujol et al., 2015; Araújo et al., 2017; Dominguez et al., 2018; Kumari et al., 2018), but the regulatory circuits that control this process are largely unknown.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: Master transcription regulators controlling biofilm formation have undergone slow substitutions over evolutionary time.
source: During that time, the master transcription regulators controlling biofilm formation have undergone slow substitutions, but their connections to the target genes they control have changed rapidly.
evidence: The claim is based on the empirical data presented in the manuscript, including ChIP-seq and gene deletion experiments.

claim: Connections between master regulators and their target genes have changed rapidly over evolutionary time.
source: During that time, the master transcription regulators controlling biofilm formation have undergone slow substitutions, but their connections to the target genes they control have changed rapidly.
evidence: The claim is based on the empirical data presented in the manuscript, including ChIP-seq experiments showing low conservation of regulator-target gene connections.

claim: The estimated divergence time for C. dubliniensis from the last common ancestor with C. albicans is approximately 20 million years.
source: The estimated divergence time for C. dubliniensis, C. tropicalis, and C. parapsilosis from the last common ancestor with C. albicans is approximately 20, 45, and 70 million years, respectively (Mishra et al., 2007; Butler et al., 2009; Moran et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Mishra et al., 2007; Butler et al., 2009; Moran et al., 2012).

claim: The estimated divergence time for C. tropicalis from the last common ancestor with C. albicans is approximately 45 million years.
source: The estimated divergence time for C. dubliniensis, C. tropicalis, and C. parapsilosis from the last common ancestor with C. albicans is approximately 20, 45, and 70 million years, respectively (Mishra et al., 2007; Butler et al., 2009; Moran et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Mishra et al., 2007; Butler et al., 2009; Moran et al., 2012).

claim: The estimated divergence time for C. parapsilosis from the last common ancestor with C. albicans is approximately 70 million years.
source: The estimated divergence time for C. dubliniensis, C. tropicalis, and C. parapsilosis from the last common ancestor with C. albicans is approximately 20, 45, and 70 million years, respectively (Mishra et al., 2007; Butler et al., 2009; Moran et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Mishra et al., 2007; Butler et al., 2009; Moran et al., 2012).

claim: Spider medium with glucose as the carbon source allowed all four species (C. albicans, C. dubliniensis, C. tropicalis, and C. parapsilosis) to form thick, well-structured biofilms.
source: We tested eight different growth media, and only Spider medium with glucose (rather than mannitol) as the carbon source allowed all four species to form thick, well-structured biofilms (Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data presented in Supplementary file 1a.

claim: C. albicans formed thick biofilms in all media tested.
source: While C. albicans formed thick biofilms in all media tested, C. tropicalis biofilm formation, for example, depended very much on carbon source (Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data presented in Supplementary file 1a.

claim: C. tropicalis biofilm formation depended very much on carbon source.
source: While C. albicans formed thick biofilms in all media tested, C. tropicalis biofilm formation, for example, depended very much on carbon source (Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data presented in Supplementary file 1a.

claim: By 48 hr, all four species (C. albicans, C. dubliniensis, C. tropicalis, and C. parapsilosis) had formed mature biofilms that did not significantly change at later time points.
source: Although C. albicans formed biofilms more rapidly, by 48 hr all four species had formed mature biofilms that did not significantly change at later time points (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Species closest to C. albicans formed the thickest biofilms, and in general, the greater the phylogenetic distance from C. albicans, the thinner the biofilm formed.
source: Although not all species were tested in the three assays, overall, of the 15 species analyzed, those closest to C. albicans formed the thickest biofilms and, in general, the greater the phylogenetic distance from C. albicans the thinner the biofilm formed (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Only C. dubliniensis and C. tropicalis formed biofilms that are structurally very similar to C. albicans biofilms, with a basal layer of yeast cells underlying a thick layer of filamentous cells (hyphae and pseudohyphae).
source: Only the two species closest to C. albicans (C. dubliniensis and C. tropicalis) formed biofilms that are structurally very similar to C. albicans biofilms, with a basal layer of yeast cells underlying a thick layer of filamentous cells (hyphae and pseudohyphae).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations described in the text and shown in figures.

claim: Biofilms formed by C. parapsilosis have a layer of filamentous cells composed largely of pseudohyphae rather than a mixture of true hyphae and pseudohyphae.
source: Biofilms formed by C. parapsilosis appeared similar at low resolution, but a closer examination showed that the layer of filamentous cells is composed largely of pseudohyphae rather than a mixture of true hyphae and pseudohyphae (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 2B.

claim: L. elongisporus formed thinner biofilms composed only of yeast cells under the tested conditions.
source: Under these conditions, Lodderomyces elongisporus formed thinner biofilms composed only of yeast cells.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations described in the text.

claim: S. passalidarum, M. guilliermondii, and C. lusitaniae form even thinner biofilms than L. elongisporus.
source: Moving further away from C. albicans, Spathaspora passalidarum, Meyerozyma guilliermondii, and Clavispora lusitaniae form even thinner biofilms, while Scheffersomyces stipites, Debaryomyces hansenii, Metschnikowia bicuspidate, Hyphopichia burtonii, and Candida tenuis did not form biofilms under the conditions we tested; only a few cells were observed adhering to the surface (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: S. stipites, D. hansenii, M. bicuspidate, H. burtonii, and C. tenuis did not form biofilms under the conditions tested; only a few cells were observed adhering to the surface.
source: Moving further away from C. albicans, Spathaspora passalidarum, Meyerozyma guilliermondii, and Clavispora lusitaniae form even thinner biofilms, while Scheffersomyces stipites, Debaryomyces hansenii, Metschnikowia bicuspidate, Hyphopichia burtonii, and Candida tenuis did not form biofilms under the conditions we tested; only a few cells were observed adhering to the surface (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: C. glabrata and S. cerevisiae did not form biofilms that resembled those formed by C. albicans and its close relatives in the assays and conditions tested.
source: As can be seen in Figure 2, neither of these species formed biofilms that resembled those formed by C. albicans and its close relatives in the assays and conditions that we tested.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: All four species (C. albicans, C. dubliniensis, C. tropicalis, and C. parapsilosis) were able to form biofilms in the rat catheter model.
source: All four species were able to form biofilms, although the biofilms formed by C. albicans and C. dubliniensis were considerably thicker and more filamentous (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The biofilms formed by C. albicans and C. dubliniensis in the rat catheter model were considerably thicker and more filamentous than those formed by C. tropicalis and C. parapsilosis.
source: All four species were able to form biofilms, although the biofilms formed by C. albicans and C. dubliniensis were considerably thicker and more filamentous (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: C. albicans biofilm formation is the most rapid and most robust to environmental changes as it formed similar biofilms in all media tested.
source: Of all the species studied, C. albicans biofilm formation is the most rapid and most robust to environmental changes as it formed similar biofilms in all media tested (Supplementary file 1a, Figure 2—figure supplement 2); moreover, the biofilms formed by this species are the most stable to physical manipulation (results not shown).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data presented in Supplementary file 1a and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The biofilms formed by C. albicans are the most stable to physical manipulation.
source: Of all the species studied, C. albicans biofilm formation is the most rapid and most robust to environmental changes as it formed similar biofilms in all media tested (Supplementary file 1a, Figure 2—figure supplement 2); moreover, the biofilms formed by this species are the most stable to physical manipulation (results not shown).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text but the supporting data is not shown.

claim: All seven master regulators of the C. albicans biofilm network have clear orthologs in C. dubliniensis, C. tropicalis, and C. parapsilosis, with the exception of Rob1.
source: All seven master regulators of the network in C. albicans (Figure 1) have clear orthologs in the other three closely related species, with the exception of Rob1.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: Rob1 has a patchy phylogenetic distribution, with syntenic orthologs present in C. albicans, C. dubliniensis, and C. tropicalis, but apparently absent from C. parapsilosis and closely related species.
source: Rob1 has a patchy phylogenetic distribution, with syntenic orthologs present in C. albicans, C. dubiniensis, and C. tropicalis, but apparently absent from C. parapsilosis and closely related species.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: Rob1 orthologs are present in other more distantly related CTG species, which supports the hypothesis that Rob1 was either lost or was evolving sufficiently rapidly in the C. parapsilosis lineage that it cannot be recognized.
source: However, Rob1 orthologs are present in other more distantly related CTG species, which supports the hypothesis that Rob1 was either lost or was evolving sufficiently rapidly in the C. parapsilosis lineage that it cannot be recognized (Maguire et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Maguire et al., 2013).

claim: All seven master regulators identified in C. albicans were also required for biofilm formation in C. dubliniensis.
source: As can be observed in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, all seven master regulators identified in C. albicans were also required for biofilm formation in C. dubliniensis.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only five of the seven master regulators (not Rob1 and Flo8) were required for biofilm formation in C. tropicalis.
source: The results were different for C. tropicalis; here, only five of the seven were required, with Rob1 and Flo8 appearing dispensable for biofilm formation under our laboratory conditions.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data described in the text and shown in figures.

claim: The biofilms formed by the rob1 and flo8 deletion mutants in C. tropicalis were actually slightly heavier and the hyphal layer was denser than biofilms formed by the parental (wildtype) strain.
source: The biofilms formed by the rob1 and flo8 deletion mutants in C. tropicalis were actually slightly heavier and the hyphal layer was denser than biofilms formed by the parental (wildtype) strain, suggesting that these two regulators may have assumed a subtle inhibitory role in this species.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations described in the text.

claim: Rob1 and Flo8 may have assumed a subtle inhibitory role in biofilm formation in C. tropicalis.
source: The biofilms formed by the rob1 and flo8 deletion mutants in C. tropicalis were actually slightly heavier and the hyphal layer was denser than biofilms formed by the parental (wildtype) strain, suggesting that these two regulators may have assumed a subtle inhibitory role in this species.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the observation that deletion mutants form thicker biofilms.

claim: For C. parapsilosis, only Bcr1 and Efg1 are indispensable for biofilm formation among the seven master biofilm regulators in C. albicans.
source: For C. parapsilosis, it was previously shown that, of the seven master biofilm regulators in C. albicans, only Bcr1 and Efg1 are indispensable for biofilm formation.
evidence: The claim is based on prior work as indicated by the phrase 'it was previously shown'.

claim: The Ndt80 deletion in C. parapsilosis fails to form biofilms but also has a general growth defect, making it difficult to ascertain its precise role.
source: The Ntd80 deletion in C. parapsilosis fails to form biofilms but also has a general growth defect, making it difficult to ascertain its precise role.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: Deletion of CZF1, UME6, CPH2, GZF3, and ACE2 all exhibit biofilm-specific defects in C. parapsilosis but not in C. albicans.
source: Previous work also established that deletion of CZF1, UME6, CPH2, GZF3, and ACE2 all exhibit biofilm-specific defects in C. parapsilosis but not in C. albicans (Holland et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Holland et al., 2014).

claim: The group of master regulators underlying biofilm formation in C. albicans is different than in other Candida species with the degree of difference roughly paralleling their evolutionary distance from C. albicans.
source: Overall, our results, together with previous observations, show that the group of master regulators underlying biofilm formation in C. albicans is different than in other Candida species with the degree of difference roughly paralleling their evolutionary distance from C. albicans.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript and prior work.

claim: The connections between master regulators and conserved target genes vary greatly across Candida species.
source: If we consider only the one-to-one orthologs, it becomes clear that the connections between master regulators and conserved target genes vary greatly across these species (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is based on ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Between C. albicans and C. dubliniensis, the master regulator that showed the highest conservation of target gene connections was Ndt80, but the overlap was only about 50% (634 of 1,297).
source: Between the two most closely related species (C. albicans and C. dubliniensis), the master regulator that showed the highest conservation of target gene connections was Ndt80, but the overlap was only about 50% (634 of 1,297).
evidence: The claim is based on ChIP-seq data analysis.

claim: Between C. albicans and C. parapsilosis, the overlap of Ndt80 target gene connections drops to about 26% (722 of 2,725).
source: Between C. albicans and C. parapsilosis, this value drops to about 26% (722 of 2,725).
evidence: The claim is based on ChIP-seq data analysis.

claim: Only 12% (371 of 3,016) of Ndt80 target gene connections are common to all four species (C. albicans, C. dubliniensis, C. tropicalis, and C. parapsilosis).
source: Although only 12% (371 of 3,016) of Ndt80 target gene connections are common to all four species, the overlap for each species pair is larger than expected by chance (hypergeometric test, p<0.05).
evidence: The claim is based on ChIP-seq data analysis and statistical testing.

claim: The overlap of Ndt80 target gene connections for each species pair is larger than expected by chance (hypergeometric test, p<0.05).
source: Although only 12% (371 of 3,016) of Ndt80 target gene connections are common to all four species, the overlap for each species pair is larger than expected by chance (hypergeometric test, p<0.05).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical testing of ChIP-seq data.

claim: Rob1 shares only about 12% (2 of 17) of its target gene connections between C. albicans and C. dubliniensis, but the overlap is still greater than expected by chance (hypergeometric test, p<0.05).
source: For example, Rob1 shares only about 12% (2 of 17) of its target gene connections between the two most related species, C. albicans and C. dubliniensis, but the overlap is still greater than expected by chance (hypergeometric test, p<0.05).
evidence: The claim is based on ChIP-seq data analysis and statistical testing.

claim: Each species has target genes in its biofilm network that lack orthologs in the other three species.
source: Our results also show that each species has target genes in its biofilm network that lack orthologs in the other three species.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of ChIP-seq data and ortholog identification.

claim: In C. albicans, 26% of the genes bound by at least one of the biofilm master regulators do not have orthologs in the other three species compared with 19% for the genome as a whole.
source: In C. albicans, 26% of the genes bound by at least one of the biofilm master regulators do not have orthologs in the other three species compared with 19% for the genome as a whole.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of ChIP-seq data and ortholog identification.

claim: Genes that are upregulated during biofilm formation in C. albicans are often 'young' genes, that is, genes that lack orthologs in related species.
source: This analysis extends the previous observation that genes that are upregulated during biofilm formation in C. albicans are often 'young' genes, that is, genes that lack orthologs in related species (Nobile et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Nobile et al., 2012) and extended by the current analysis.

claim: A similar enrichment of unique genes in the biofilm network was observed in C. parapsilosis, but not for C. dubliniensis and C. tropicalis.
source: We observed a similar enrichment of unique genes in the biofilm network of C. parapsilosis, but not for C. dubliniensis and C. tropicalis; in the latter two species, the fraction of non-orthologous genes in the biofilm network was approximately the same as that observed for the whole genome.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of ChIP-seq data and ortholog identification.

claim: The biofilm networks of C. albicans and C. parapsilosis have been more dynamic in recent evolutionary time than those of C. dubliniensis and C. tropicalis.
source: These observations indicate that the biofilm networks of C. albicans and C. parapsilosis have been more dynamic in recent evolutionary time than those of the other two species.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that C. albicans and C. parapsilosis have more unique genes in their biofilm networks.

claim: The binding motif for some of the master regulators does not vary significantly across the species studied.
source: As discussed below, the binding motif for some of the master regulators does not vary significantly across the species we studied.
evidence: The claim is based on de novo motif analysis of ChIP-seq data.

claim: The high proportion of differences in regulator-target gene connections across Candida species did not significantly change when the stringency of the filtering criteria increased.
source: Although the gross number of regulator-target gene connections decreased as the stringency of the filtering criteria increased, the high proportion of differences across Candida species described above did not significantly change (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of ChIP-seq data with different filtering criteria, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The binding intensities of Ndt80 in all the intergenic regions of the genome were highly correlated between the two media tested (Spider 1% glucose and alternative media) in C. albicans, C. dubliniensis, and C. tropicalis.
source: In all species, the binding intensities of the regulator in all the intergenic regions of the genome were highly correlated between the two media tested (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is based on ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: There are no significant changes in Ndt80 binding when the growth media is modified.
source: This finding indicates that there are no significant changes in Ndt80 binding when the growth media is modified.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the high correlation of binding intensities between different media.

claim: Many target genes were directly connected (by binding) to more than one master regulator in C. albicans.
source: The initial characterization of the biofilm transcription circuit in C. albicans showed that many target genes were directly connected (by binding) to more than one master regulator (Nobile et al., 2012), and this general feature of the network architecture is observed across the Candida species studied here, despite the low conservation of individual regulator-target gene connections (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Nobile et al., 2012) and extended by the current analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: High connectivity of the biofilm network is observed across the Candida species studied, despite the low conservation of individual regulator-target gene connections.
source: The initial characterization of the biofilm transcription circuit in C. albicans showed that many target genes were directly connected (by binding) to more than one master regulator (Nobile et al., 2012), and this general feature of the network architecture is observed across the Candida species studied here, despite the low conservation of individual regulator-target gene connections (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is based on ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Over 75% of the Efg1 target genes are also Ndt80 targets in all four species.
source: The set of target genes of Ndt80 is considerably larger, but over 75% of the Efg1 target genes are also Ndt80 targets in all four species.
evidence: The claim is based on ChIP-seq data analysis.

claim: The binding motifs of Ndt80 and Efg1 are enriched in each other's binding locations in all four species studied.
source: In addition, the binding motifs of these two regulators are enriched in each other's binding locations in all four species studied (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is based on motif analysis of ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In all species, Efg1 binds in conjunction with Ndt80 even though the target genes of the regulator combination differ greatly across species.
source: These observations indicate that, in all species, Efg1 binds in conjunction with Ndt80 even though the target genes of the regulator combination differ greatly across species.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that Efg1 and Ndt80 binding motifs are enriched in each other's binding locations.

claim: The association between Efg1 and Ndt80 agrees with previous planktonic ChIP-seq experiments of Efg1 performed in C. parapsilosis where the most enriched binding motif found was that of Ndt80.
source: The association between Efg1 and Ndt80 agrees with previous planktonic ChIP-seq experiments of Efg1 performed in C. parapsilosis where the most enriched binding motif found was that of Ndt80 (Connolly et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Connolly et al., 2013).

claim: The DNA-binding motifs of Efg1 and Ndt80 have been shown to co-occur in the binding regions of Sfl1 and Sfl2, two regulators of filamentation in C. albicans.
source: The DNA-binding motifs of these two regulators have also been shown to co-occur in the binding regions of Sfl1 and Sfl2, two regulators of filamentation in C. albicans (Znaidi et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Znaidi et al., 2013).

claim: The Efg1-Ndt80 association is ancient with respect to the Candida species studied and remains preserved across them despite large species-to-species differences in the target genes bound by the two regulators.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that the Efg1-Ndt80 association is ancient with respect to the Candida species studied here and that it remains preserved across them despite large species-to-species differences in the target genes bound by the two regulators.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that Efg1 and Ndt80 binding motifs co-occur across species and in prior work.

claim: Combinational control of target genes is very common in all species.
source: Analysis of the other master regulators indicates that combinational control of target genes is very common in all species, although the other examples do not seem as deeply conserved as the Efg1-Ndt8o example.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of ChIP-seq data for multiple regulators.

claim: Ndt80 shows the highest conservation of binding connections between one master regulator and the others.
source: The extent of conservation of the binding connections between one master regulator and the others varies from regulator to regulator (Supplementary file 1c), with Ndt80 showing the highest conservation.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of ChIP-seq data presented in Supplementary file 1c.

claim: In all four species, Ndt80 binds to its own control region as well as those of all six other regulators, with the exception of the control region of FLO8 in C. albicans and ROB1 in C. dubliniensis.
source: In all four species, Ndt80 binds to its own control region as well as those of all six other regulators, with the exception of the control region of FLO8 in C. albicans and ROB1 in C. dubliniensis.
evidence: The claim is based on ChIP-seq data analysis.

claim: Ndt80 and Efg1 each bind to their own control regions in all four species analyzed.
source: Ndt80 and Efg1 each bind to their own control regions in all the four species analyzed, while Brg1 exhibits this interaction only in C. albicans and C. dubliniensis.
evidence: The claim is based on ChIP-seq data analysis.

claim: Brg1 binds to its own control region only in C. albicans and C. dubliniensis.
source: Ndt80 and Efg1 each bind to their own control regions in all the four species analyzed, while Brg1 exhibits this interaction only in C. albicans and C. dubliniensis.
evidence: The claim is based on ChIP-seq data analysis.

claim: High connectivity between the master regulators is conserved in the four Candida species analyzed.
source: Overall, our findings show that high connectivity between the master regulators is conserved in the four Candida species analyzed.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of ChIP-seq data.

claim: Despite the extensive changes in the network across species, the high connectivity among regulators remains a structural feature of the network in each species.
source: Thus, despite the extensive changes in the network across species, the high connectivity among regulators remains a structural feature of the network in each species.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that high connectivity is conserved despite changes in individual connections.

claim: The enriched DNA-binding motifs found in the binding regions of the biofilm master regulators were very similar across the four species examined.
source: Performing de novo motif searches, we found that the enriched DNA-binding motifs found in the binding regions of the biofilm master regulators were very similar across the four species we examined (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is based on de novo motif analysis of ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The de novo generated DNA-binding motifs for Efg1 and Ndt80 are similar to those previously reported for their orthologs in C. albicans and other species.
source: Moreover, the de novo generated DNA-binding motifs for Efg1 and Ndt80 are similar to those previously reported for their orthologs in C. albicans and other species (Nobile et al., 2012; Nocedal et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Nobile et al., 2012; Nocedal et al., 2017).

claim: The overlap of potential targets between species based on motif scoring varied from 51 to 100% depending on the exact motif used, but was never low enough to account for the differences determined directly from the ChIP-seq experiments.
source: The overlap of potential targets between species varied from 51 to 100% depending on the exact motif used, but was never low enough to account for the differences determined directly from the ChIP-seq experiments (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is based on motif analysis and comparison with ChIP-seq data.

claim: The large differences in regulator-target interactions across species observed in the ChIP-seq data cannot be accounted for by slight differences in the binding motifs generated in each individual species.
source: In other words, the large differences in regulator-target interactions across species observed in the ChIP-seq data cannot be accounted for by slight differences in the binding motifs generated in each individual species.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that motif-based predictions do not explain the observed differences in ChIP-seq data.

claim: The DNA-binding specificity of at least some of the master regulators has not changed significantly across these species.
source: Although we cannot fully disregard that small differences in binding affinity contribute to differences in master regulator-target gene connections observed across the species, overall, all the analyses show that the DNA-binding specificity of at least some of the master regulators has not changed significantly across these species.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on motif analysis and ChIP-seq data.

claim: The pairwise differences in the transcription profiles across the three species (C. albicans, C. dubliniensis, and C. tropicalis) are significant and reflect their phylogenetic position: the further apart the two species are from one another, the less correlated their transcription profiles are.
source: As seen in Figure 5B, the pairwise differences in the transcription profiles across the three species are significant and reflect their phylogenetic position: the further apart the two species are from one another, the less correlated their transcription profiles are.
evidence: The claim is based on transcription profiling data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Only 29% of the genes that change their expression during biofilm formation are shared between C. albicans and C. dubliniensis (using a twofold cutoff).
source: If we use a lax cutoff of twofold over/underexpression to define genes that change their expression during biofilm formation, the overlap between pairs of species is relatively low. For example, only 29% of the genes that change their expression during biofilm formation are shared between C. albicans and C. dubliniensis, and only 24% are shared between C. albicans and C. tropicalis.
evidence: The claim is based on transcription profiling data analysis.

claim: Only 24% of the genes that change their expression during biofilm formation are shared between C. albicans and C. tropicalis (using a twofold cutoff).
source: If we use a lax cutoff of twofold over/underexpression to define genes that change their expression during biofilm formation, the overlap between pairs of species is relatively low. For example, only 29% of the genes that change their expression during biofilm formation are shared between C. albicans and C. dubliniensis, and only 24% are shared between C. albicans and C. tropicalis.
evidence: The claim is based on transcription profiling data analysis.

claim: The overlap of differentially expressed genes between the two C. albicans isolates was 48%.
source: The overlap of differentially expressed genes between the two C. albicans isolates was 48%.
evidence: The claim is based on transcription profiling data analysis.

claim: Clinical isolates differ in their biofilm-forming abilities.
source: This result is consistent with previous work showing that clinical isolates differ in their biofilm-forming abilities (Hirakawa et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Hirakawa et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2019).

claim: All the interspecific pairwise overlaps of differentially expressed genes are greater than would be expected by chance (hypergeometric test, p<<0.05).
source: Despite these major differences, all the interspecific pairwise overlaps are greater than would be expected by chance (hypergeometric test, p<<0.05), although we cannot distinguish if this is due primarily to selection or to the shared ancestry of their promoter sequences.
evidence: The claim is based on statistical testing of transcription profiling data.

claim: The low degree of conservation in genome-wide gene expression agrees well with the low conservation of regulator-target gene connections across species.
source: Overall, the low degree of conservation in genome-wide gene expression agrees well with the low conservation of regulator-target gene connections across species described above.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the comparison of gene expression and ChIP-seq data.

claim: The fraction of differentially expressed genes bound by one or more regulators ranges from 30% in C. albicans to 51% in C. tropicalis.
source: Considering genes that change their expression at least twofold during biofilm formation in the same conditions in which the ChIP-seq experiments were performed, the fraction of these genes bound by one or more regulators ranges from 30% in C. albicans to 51% in C. tropicalis.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of ChIP-seq and transcription profiling data.

claim: 67% of differently expressed genes in C. parapsilosis were bound by at least one of the biofilm regulators under the experimental conditions tested.
source: Combining our data with previous transcriptional profiling experiments performed in C. parapsilosis during biofilm formation (Holland et al., 2014), we estimated that 67% of differently expressed genes in this species were bound by at least one of the biofilm regulators under the experimental conditions tested.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of ChIP-seq data and prior transcription profiling data (Holland et al., 2014).

claim: The overlap between differential gene expression and regulator binding in all species is larger than what would be expected by chance (hypergeometric test, p<<0.05), suggesting that direct binding is an important factor in gene regulation in the biofilm network.
source: The overlap between differential gene expression and regulator binding in all species is larger than what would be expected by chance (hypergeometric test, p<<0.05), suggesting that direct binding is an important factor in gene regulation in the biofilm network.
evidence: The claim is based on statistical testing of ChIP-seq and transcription profiling data.

claim: Most genes that are expressed differentially between species are genes whose intergenic region is bound by at least one regulator in one species, but not in the other species.
source: Pairwise comparisons of C. albicans, C. dubliniensis, and C. tropicalis showed that most genes that are expressed differentially between species (as defined above) are genes whose intergenic region is bound by at least one regulator in one species, but not in the other species.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of ChIP-seq and transcription profiling data.

claim: This association is statistically significant (Fisher's two-tailed exact test, p<<0.05) suggesting that the majority of differences in biofilm-specific gene expression between species can be explained by differences in the cis-regulatory sequences of target genes that alter binding of the regulators.
source: This association is statistically significant (Fisher's two-tailed exact test, p<<0.05) again suggesting that the majority of differences in biofilm-specific gene expression between species can be explained by differences in the cis-regulatory sequences of target genes that alter binding of the regulators.
evidence: The claim is based on statistical testing of ChIP-seq and transcription profiling data.

claim: C. albicans and C. dubliniensis can be mated to generate tetraploid hybrids.
source: We took advantage of the fact that it is possible to mate C. albicans and C. dubliniensis (each diploid) to generate tetraploid hybrids (Pujol et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Pujol et al., 2004).

claim: C. albicans-C. dubliniensis hybrids form biofilms similar to those formed by C. albicans.
source: These hybrids form biofilms similar to those formed by C. albicans (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the C. albicans-C. dubliniensis hybrid, the target genes bound by the C. albicans Ndt80 and the C. dubliniensis Ndt80 were highly correlated, similar to two biological replicates carried out in the same species.
source: The results showed that — in the hybrid — the target genes bound by the C. albicans Ndt80 and the C. dubliniensis Ndt80 were highly correlated, similar to two biological replicates carried out in the same species (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is based on ChIP-seq data in the hybrid shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In the hybrid, the same target genes were obtained regardless of which Ndt80 was tagged for immunoprecipitation.
source: In other words, we obtained the same target genes in the hybrid regardless of which Ndt80 was tagged for immunoprecipitation.
evidence: The claim is based on ChIP-seq data in the hybrid.

claim: The binding positions on the C. dubliniensis genome in the hybrid were characteristic of the results in C. dubliniensis, specifically 97% of the targets in the hybrid are targets in C. dubliniensis.
source: Importantly, the binding positions on the C. dubliniensis genome in the hybrid were characteristic of the results in C. dubliniensis, specifically 97% of the targets in the hybrid are targets in C. dubliniensis, and the positions on the C. albicans genome were characteristic of C. albicans with 96% of the targets in the hybrid being targets in C. albicans.
evidence: The claim is based on ChIP-seq data in the hybrid.

claim: The binding positions on the C. albicans genome in the hybrid were characteristic of C. albicans with 96% of the targets in the hybrid being targets in C. albicans.
source: Importantly, the binding positions on the C. dubliniensis genome in the hybrid were characteristic of the results in C. dubliniensis, specifically 97% of the targets in the hybrid are targets in C. dubliniensis, and the positions on the C. albicans genome were characteristic of C. albicans with 96% of the targets in the hybrid being targets in C. albicans.
evidence: The claim is based on ChIP-seq data in the hybrid.

claim: The extreme differences in regulator-target gene connections observed across these Candida species are due to changes in the cis-regulatory sequences in the target genes rather than changes in the regulators themselves or differences in the physiological state of the species at the time of analysis.
source: These observations confirm our previous conclusion that the extreme differences in regulator-target gene connections observed across these Candida species are due to changes in the cis-regulatory sequences in the target genes rather than changes in the regulators themselves or differences in the physiological state of the species at the time of analysis.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the hybrid ChIP-seq data.

claim: As we move away from C. albicans, biofilms become less complex, both in terms of structure and of composition; that is, fewer cell types are involved and the resulting biofilm is less regular.
source: (1) As we move away from C. albicans, biofilms become less complex, both in terms of structure and of composition; that is, fewer cell types are involved and the resulting biofilm is less regular.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations described in the manuscript.

claim: At larger evolutionary distances, fungal species did not form biofilms at all under the conditions tested.
source: At larger evolutionary distances, fungal species did not form biofilms at all under the conditions we tested.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations described in the manuscript.

claim: Of the seven master transcriptional regulators of biofilm formation in C. albicans, all seven are needed in C. dubliniensis.
source: (2) Of the seven master transcriptional regulators of biofilm formation in C. albicans, all seven are needed in the most closely related species (C. dubliniensis), but, as we move further away evolutionarily, fewer are required for biofilm formation.
evidence: The claim is based on gene deletion experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: As we move further away evolutionarily from C. albicans, fewer master regulators are required for biofilm formation.
source: (2) Of the seven master transcriptional regulators of biofilm formation in C. albicans, all seven are needed in the most closely related species (C. dubliniensis), but, as we move further away evolutionarily, fewer are required for biofilm formation.
evidence: The claim is based on gene deletion experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Two of the master regulators (Rob1 and Flo8) are dispensable for biofilm formation in C. tropicalis.
source: For example, two of the master regulators (Rob1 and Flo8) are dispensable for biofilm formation in the next most closely related species (C. tropicalis), and three of the seven are not required in C. parapsilosis.
evidence: The claim is based on gene deletion experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Three of the seven master regulators are not required for biofilm formation in C. parapsilosis.
source: For example, two of the master regulators (Rob1 and Flo8) are dispensable for biofilm formation in the next most closely related species (C. tropicalis), and three of the seven are not required in C. parapsilosis.
evidence: The claim is based on gene deletion experiments and prior work.

claim: Other transcriptional regulators (present in C. albicans but not required for biofilm formation in this species) have assumed the role of master regulators in C. parapsilosis.
source: As shown by Holland and colleagues (Holland et al., 2014), other transcriptional regulators (present in C. albicans but not required for biofilm formation in this species) have assumed the role of master regulators in C. parapsilosis.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Holland et al., 2014).

claim: The differences in regulator-target gene connections across species are due largely to changes in the cis-regulatory sequences of the target genes rather than changes in the regulators.
source: This result strongly supports the conclusion that the differences in regulator-target gene connections across species are due largely to changes in the cis-regulatory sequences of the target genes rather than changes in the regulators.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the hybrid ChIP-seq data.

claim: mRNA expression during biofilm formation differs considerably from one species to the next.
source: (4) As predicted from the extensive changes in regulator-target gene connections, mRNA expression during biofilm formation differs considerably from one species to the next.
evidence: The claim is based on transcription profiling data described in the manuscript.

claim: mRNA expression divergence becomes greater as the phylogenetic distance increases.
source: Like the other changes we have documented in this paper, mRNA expression divergence becomes greater as the phylogenetic distance increases (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is based on transcription profiling data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Despite the extensive changes in the transcription networks underlying biofilm formation across the species examined, several key features of the overall architecture of the network appear to be preserved.
source: (5) Despite the extensive changes in the transcription networks underlying biofilm formation across the species we examined, several key features of the overall architecture of the network appear to be preserved.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the analysis of ChIP-seq data.

claim: All species show high connectivity in the sense that many target genes are directly connected (by binding) to more than one master regulator.
source: For example, all species show high connectivity in the sense that many target genes are directly connected (by binding) to more than one master regulator.
evidence: The claim is based on ChIP-seq data analysis.

claim: The high connectivity observed is dominated by the DNA binding of Ndt80 and Efg1.
source: The high connectivity observed is dominated by the DNA binding of Ndt80 and Efg1, and we note that these regulators are also involved in several other cellular functions and have been suggested to cooperatively regulate their target genes (Sellam et al., 2010; Znaidi et al., 2013; Mancera et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on ChIP-seq data analysis and supported by citations to prior work (Sellam et al., 2010; Znaidi et al., 2013; Mancera et al., 2015).

claim: Ndt80 and Efg1 are involved in several other cellular functions and have been suggested to cooperatively regulate their target genes.
source: The high connectivity observed is dominated by the DNA binding of Ndt80 and Efg1, and we note that these regulators are also involved in several other cellular functions and have been suggested to cooperatively regulate their target genes (Sellam et al., 2010; Znaidi et al., 2013; Mancera et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Sellam et al., 2010; Znaidi et al., 2013; Mancera et al., 2015).

claim: Many of the master regulators bind to their own control regions as well as those of the other master regulators.
source: Moreover, many of the master regulators bind to their own control regions as well as those of the other master regulators.
evidence: The claim is based on ChIP-seq data analysis.

claim: High connectivity and self-regulation are likely to be common to many complex transcription networks.
source: We have argued elsewhere that these two features are likely to be common to many complex transcription networks (Sorrells and Johnson, 2015), and the results presented here show that, despite many changes in individual regulator-target connections, the basic 'structural features' of the network are preserved across the biofilm networks of the four species examined.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Sorrells and Johnson, 2015) and extended by the current analysis.

claim: Despite many changes in individual regulator-target connections, the basic 'structural features' of the network are preserved across the biofilm networks of the four species examined.
source: We have argued elsewhere that these two features are likely to be common to many complex transcription networks (Sorrells and Johnson, 2015), and the results presented here show that, despite many changes in individual regulator-target connections, the basic 'structural features' of the network are preserved across the biofilm networks of the four species examined.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the analysis of ChIP-seq data.

claim: Specific master regulator-target gene connections that are preserved across multiple species may point to target genes that are notably important for biofilm formation in these Candida species.
source: For example, specific master regulator-target gene connections that are preserved across multiple species may point to target genes that are notably important for biofilm formation in these Candida species.
evidence: The claim is speculative, suggesting a hypothesis for future work.

claim: Hirakawa et al., 2015 determined the genome sequences of 21 clinical isolates of C. albicans and examined their abilities to form biofilms.
source: Hirakawa et al., 2015 determined the genome sequences of 21 clinical isolates of C. albicans and examined their abilities to form biofilms.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Hirakawa et al., 2015).

claim: Among the strains analyzed by Hirakawa et al., 2015, the strain used in this study (SC5314) was among the thickest biofilm producers as assayed by dry weight; the majority of isolates formed thinner biofilms.
source: Among the strains analyzed, the one used in our study (SC5314) was among the thickest biofilm producers as assayed by dry weight; the majority of isolates formed thinner biofilms.
evidence: The claim is based on prior work (Hirakawa et al., 2015).

claim: One clinical isolate that formed very poor biofilms was found to have an inactivating mutation in EFG1, one of the biofilm master regulators, indicating a relatively recent change.
source: One clinical isolate that formed very poor biofilms was found to have an inactivating mutation in EFG1, one of the biofilm master regulators, indicating a relatively recent change.
evidence: The claim is based on prior work (Hirakawa et al., 2015).

claim: SC5314 is a good representative of C. albicans and most of the clinical isolates probably acquired mutations (including aneuploidies and losses of heterozygosity) relatively recently.
source: Because the C. dubliniensis strain used in our study (CD36) formed biofilms that are similar to those of strain SC5314, we believe that SC5314 is a good representative of C. albicans and that most of the clinical isolates probably acquired mutations (including aneuploidies and losses of heterozygosity) relatively recently.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the comparison of biofilm phenotypes.

claim: Huang et al., 2019 examined five of the previously sequenced strains in much more detail including the dependence on individual transcriptional regulators for biofilm formation.
source: Huang et al., 2019 examined five of the previously sequenced strains in much more detail including the dependence on individual transcriptional regulators for biofilm formation.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Huang et al., 2019).

claim: Although the magnitude of the effect of transcriptional regulator deletions on biofilm formation varied across strains, SC5314 appears to be a good representation of the ability of C. albicans as a species to form thick, complex biofilms.
source: Although the magnitude of the effect of transcriptional regulator deletions on biofilm formation varied across strains, SC5314 again appears to be a good representation of the ability of C. albicans as a species to form thick, complex biofilms.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on prior work (Huang et al., 2019).

claim: This study is the first to examine in detail how a complex transcription network changes over a relatively short evolutionary time — 70 million years — represented by four different species.
source: To our knowledge, this study is the first to examine in detail how a complex transcription network changes over a relatively short evolutionary time — 70 million years — represented by four different species.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: Although the biofilms produced by the Candida species have many similarities, they do differ from species to species in at least subtle aspects.
source: We do not know which, if any, of these changes were adaptive; in this regard, it is important to note that, although the biofilms produced by the Candida species have many similarities, they do differ from species to species in at least subtle aspects.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations described in the manuscript.

claim: Although C. albicans and C. dubliniensis biofilms appear very similar under the confocal microscope, the C. albicans biofilms form faster and under a greater range of conditions; once formed, they are more difficult to disrupt than those of C. dubliniensis.
source: Even considering the two most closely related species (C. albicans and C. dubliniensis), it is possible to distinguish their biofilms. Although they appear very similar under the confocal microscope, the C. albicans biofilms form faster and under a greater range of conditions; once formed, they are more difficult to disrupt than those of C. dubliniensis.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations described in the manuscript.

claim: It is difficult to reconcile the subtle differences in biofilm phenotype with the large differences in the underlying transcriptional circuitry.
source: Although these differences may help to explain why C. albicans is a greater problem in the clinic than C. dubliniensis, it is difficult to reconcile these subtle differences in phenotype with the large differences in the underlying transcriptional circuitry.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the comparison of phenotypic and molecular data.

claim: Many of the changes in transcription circuitry result from neutral evolution, more specifically, constructive neutral evolution whereby molecular complexity can change without an increase in fitness.
source: Given the large magnitude of changes underlying such similar phenotypic output, we propose as a default hypothesis that many of the changes in transcription circuitry result from neutral evolution, more specifically, constructive neutral evolution whereby molecular complexity can change without an increase in fitness (Stoltzfus, 1999; Lynch, 2007; Wagner, 2014; Sorrells and Johnson, 2015; Brunet and Doolittle, 2018).
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis supported by citations to prior work (Stoltzfus, 1999; Lynch, 2007; Wagner, 2014; Sorrells and Johnson, 2015; Brunet and Doolittle, 2018).

claim: Complex transcription networks responsible for the same basic phenotype can undergo evolutionary changes that appear much greater in magnitude than the resulting differences in phenotype.
source: This study clearly shows that complex transcription networks responsible for the same basic phenotype can undergo evolutionary changes that appear much greater in magnitude than the resulting differences in phenotype.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the data presented in the manuscript.
